rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google just launched Gemini 4 Carbon — and the first people who get to use it aren't developers, aren't businesses. They're cyber defenders. Specific ones. A small, vetted group.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a strange guest list for a product launch.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Staged access. Which means Google has decided trust is the product, not just the model.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's worth understanding. Stay with us.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: You're listening to The AI Edge, Thursday, October 29th, 2026. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. Today: a frontier model built for security, a financial signal from two of the biggest spenders in tech, and a coding tool that decides which AI handles your code so you don't have to.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. When AI news moves this fast, knowing what happened is not enough; you need to know what changes your next decision. The Ledger turns the day’s noise into five focused briefings for people who need the consequence before consensus catches up. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So. Gemini 4 Carbon. Google DeepMind announced it yesterday, October 28th. And I want to start with the obvious question — is this just Gemini 4 Argon with a different element name, or did something actually change?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Something actually changed. Argon was a general frontier model. Carbon is positioned specifically around cybersecurity and what Google calls long-horizon agentic tasks. That's not just a rebrand.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Long-horizon agentic — unpack that for me.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Think of a task that takes dozens of steps, where the AI has to plan ahead, hold context across a lot of information, and keep working without you checking in every thirty seconds. Vulnerability scanning, patching sequences, threat investigation. Not one question, one answer. More like: here's a problem — go solve it and come back when it's done.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is exactly why the access is staged. You don't hand that kind of autonomy to everyone at once.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right, so who's actually in the room right now?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A subset of cyber defenders. Google described it as starting with a select group this week, then expanding to what they're calling the Fairwind Program — trusted partners — before any broader developer, business, or consumer rollout.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Fairwind Program.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Every enterprise launch needs a name that sounds like a yacht club.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm not wrong. But the function is serious — it's how Google controls who stress-tests the model before it meets the general public.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that caution or is that just keeping a competitive advantage locked up while they test marketing?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Could be both. But there's a legitimate safety argument here. If you're building a model that can autonomously hunt for security vulnerabilities, you do not want to discover its edge cases at scale. You find out with a controlled group first.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The guardrail testing is explicitly stated in Google's announcement. They said they'll continue that before the wider release.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, so what does Carbon actually do that's different in a security context?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Google says it's their strongest model yet for cybersecurity defense. The specific claim is that it's built for both cybersecurity tasks and those long-horizon workflows I mentioned. Now — and this is a vendor claim, so we hold it at arm's length — that's what they're positioning it as. We haven't seen independent benchmarks yet.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. There's no outside test saying "yes, Carbon finds zero-days faster."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Not yet. That's exactly what security teams will be watching for.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And there's a revealing number in the pricing that I think tells you more about Google's actual bet here than the product copy does.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The cached input discount?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Ninety-five percent off cached input tokens. The base pricing is two dollars per million input tokens, ten dollars per million output tokens — which is in line with where frontier models have been sitting. But the cache discount is striking.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That jumped out at me immediately. Caching, for listeners who haven't hit this — when you send a lot of the same background information to a model repeatedly, the system stores it so you're not paying to re-process it every single time. It's like having a really long document on file versus reading it out loud each time you call.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And ninety-five percent off that is enormous.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's enormous. And it tells you Google expects Carbon to be used in repetitive, structured workflows — running the same security policy documents, the same codebase, the same threat intel feed through the model over and over. Not one-off queries.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is exactly what an enterprise security team does. They're not asking novel philosophical questions. They're running continuous scans against a known environment.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the pricing is almost a design document.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a nice way to put it. Yes.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It also, frankly, makes Carbon more attractive against competitors at the same tier. If your security team is running this at volume, ninety-five percent off the repetitive parts changes the economics considerably.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And it's launching at the same introductory price as Argon, according to Google.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right. They're not using a new model as an excuse to raise prices at the gate. Whether that holds as access expands is a different question.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I'm still turning over — Carbon builds on Argon, Google says it's designed for cybersecurity defense. But what does that actually mean architecturally? Is it fine-tuned on security data, or is "cybersecurity-focused" just the use case they're marketing it toward?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the question I can't fully answer from what Google's released. They haven't specified the training methodology publicly. The design claim is real. The mechanism behind it isn't confirmed.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which matters quite a lot if you're a security team deciding whether to request early access. "Optimized for" could mean deeply specialized or it could mean "we ran some security benchmarks and liked the numbers."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Not yet. Though the cache discount does point at something specific: you don't price for repetitive long-horizon workflows unless the model can actually hold a long context window without losing the thread of what it found three steps ago. That would be the real architectural distinction — and that's what the defender cohort will either confirm or complicate.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Context window — that's how much the model can hold in working memory at once?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Essentially. If Carbon can maintain coherence across a long threat investigation without losing the thread of what it found three steps ago, that's a real capability distinction. If it can't, the workflow falls apart regardless of the pricing.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that's precisely what the initial defender cohort will stress-test before anyone else sees it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the staged rollout is also the evaluation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a neat way to think about it. Yes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Here's the thing I keep coming back to. We're in a moment where "AI for cybersecurity" is being said by approximately everyone. What makes this different from a security-themed marketing layer?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The honest answer is we don't fully know yet. The architecture claim is real — long-horizon task design is a genuine technical distinction. The pricing structure is real. The staged rollout is real. Whether it actually shortens the time between spotting a vulnerability and patching it in a live environment — that's what the cyber defender cohort is going to find out.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that's worth watching. Because if the initial group reports meaningful improvements, the expansion to the Fairwind partners will happen quickly. If the results are mixed, you'll see that rollout slow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what's the signal to watch?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Speed of the rollout. If Google moves to trusted partners fast — within weeks — that's a sign the internal feedback is good. If it sits at the defender cohort for a long time, read that as evidence the guardrail testing found something.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And watch whether independent security researchers get access. That's when you get credible third-party results rather than testimonials from partners who signed a program agreement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fair. Our second story.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google had other news yesterday, and this one's about money rather than models. Both Google and Microsoft reported Q3 earnings, and both declined to raise their capital expenditure forecasts for the next quarter.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which sounds like a nothing story until you understand what they've actually been spending.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk us through it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So capex — capital expenditure — for these companies is mostly what they spend building data centers: physical servers, power infrastructure, cooling systems. For two years, Google and Microsoft have been doing this at historically aggressive rates. Analysts kept expecting the numbers to climb. They didn't.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They held steady. And in a market that has spent two years pricing in perpetual growth, "held steady" reads as a signal.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture a quieter office in midtown Manhattan — not a trading floor, just a lot of screens showing earnings transcripts and Q3 slides. This is where institutional investors were watching Google and Microsoft report on October 29th. These are people with real money parked in the AI infrastructure thesis: buy the companies building the picks-and-shovels — ride the spend wave. And what they heard was — the wave is not accelerating. Google held capex steady. Microsoft held capex steady. The question immediately on every desk was whether this is prudent maturation or the first sign that revenue isn't coming in fast enough to justify more. CNBC called it the AI build-out hitting a snag. That's not neutral language. The market expected growth and got discipline instead.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But discipline from a company sitting on billions in existing infrastructure isn't the same as weakness.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Correct. Which is exactly what makes the next few quarters interesting. The question isn't whether they can build more data centers. It's whether investors believe existing capacity will generate the revenue that justifies everything already built.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. So who does this actually hurt?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If you supply chips, power, or cooling to those data centers, a pause in forecast growth is not neutral — you were pricing in more contracts.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And for anyone watching the broader sector, it confirms something that's been building: the "build at any cost" phase is now under real investor pressure. Analysts are explicitly asking for clearer revenue returns on existing spend.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does slowing capex growth affect what models they can actually build?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Not in the short term. Both companies have enormous infrastructure already deployed. You don't need to announce a new data center to run the models you've already committed to.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What it affects is the timeline for the next generation. If you're not expanding aggressively now, you're potentially pushing out the capacity needed for the model generation after this one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So something we see in 2027 or 2028 might be shaped by a decision made in this earnings call.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Possibly. With the qualification that we don't yet know if this is a one-quarter pause or a genuine reset. CNBC characterizes it as a cautious approach and specifically notes it doesn't constitute a permanent halt.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I'll say — yesterday I joked I was relieved we might get through a week without another ten-billion-dollar data center announcement. And now I'm slightly worried the version of the AI future I was imagining might just be delayed.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the correct amount of ambivalence for this story.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Heh. The market is shifting its vocabulary. For two years the question was "how much are you spending?" Now it's "what are you getting for it?" That's a considerably more demanding question.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What should listeners actually be watching?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Next quarter's guidance from both companies. If either signals a return to capex growth, this was a pause. If they hold steady again, it's a strategy. And watch whether smaller cloud providers — who have less cushion — start feeling the pressure first.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And watch whether the efficiency push filters down to models. If the giants are demanding more from existing infrastructure, that creates real pressure to build leaner. Which might actually benefit the end user eventually.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a quietly hopeful reading of a story that doesn't feel hopeful on the surface.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'll take it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I wouldn't take it too fast. The investor pressure coming in the next few quarters is going to be real, and it's going to be loud.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, another hundred AI headlines before breakfast? People have actual work to do. How do they decide what deserves their attention?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: With The Ledger, Jamie. A longer reading list is hardly a strategy. Five focused briefings help connect the news to decisions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So The Ledger gives you a place to start asking better questions about your work and your team?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Precisely. The Ledger. Find the link in our show notes. Now, back to the discussion.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story is about coding tools, and specifically about a new thing GitHub launched today called Copilot Fusion.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I love this one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Tell me why, because I've been going back and forth on it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay so — the idea is that instead of every coding task going through a single AI model, Copilot Fusion dynamically routes each task to the best available model based on what that task actually needs. Simple autocomplete? Small cheap model. Complex architecture problem? Bigger, more capable model. The system makes that call.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So it's like a traffic router for AI.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. The routing happens automatically — you're not sitting there choosing which model handles which line of code.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And who's doing the routing? That's what I can't get comfortable with.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: GitHub's system. The logic decides which model is most efficient for a given task based on complexity and cost.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: But efficient for whom? For my code quality, or for GitHub's compute bill?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And there it is.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is a genuinely good question and we don't have a definitive answer. GitHub's stated goal is to optimize for both quality and cost reduction. The reported mechanism is that it matches model capability to task complexity — more demanding task, more capable model.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right, but I'm trusting that the routing criteria aligns with what I actually need, not what's cheapest to serve me.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is — and I say this not cynically but practically — exactly what every enterprise software platform promises. The interesting question is whether there's any transparency about which model handled your code.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That we don't know from the current reporting.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And it requires an active GitHub Copilot subscription to use at all.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So Microsoft — which owns GitHub — has built a multi-model selection system that runs inside a subscription tier they control. That's not a criticism, but it is a structure.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Although — can I defend the actual utility for a second?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Please.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Imagine you're a developer and in the course of a single morning you write a short test function, refactor a complex authentication module, and then ask the assistant to explain a gnarly piece of legacy code someone else wrote. Those are wildly different tasks in terms of what they need from an AI. The idea that one model handles all three identically is actually the strange assumption. Routing makes intuitive sense.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, that does make sense. The question is just whether I know what's happening.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And whether the promised cost savings materialize. GitHub says it reduces compute overhead by matching models to tasks. But the performance depends on which models are integrated, and we don't have independent results yet — just the launch announcement.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: There's also something worth noting here in the context of the earlier story. We just talked about Microsoft holding capex steady. Copilot Fusion is partly an answer to why: if you can serve more developer tasks per unit of compute by routing efficiently, you don't need to keep adding raw capacity at the same rate.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The efficiency is the point.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Oh. That actually connects.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I was wondering when you'd get there.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I know. I'm delighted every time.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The routing logic is the thing I'd want to see opened up. Not necessarily open-source, but some kind of explanation: here's what we optimized for, here's how the decision was made. Developers are generally more comfortable when they understand the tool.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And from a practical standpoint — if you're already on GitHub Copilot, this is just available to you. You're not adding a subscription.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. It's a new capability within the existing subscription. The question of whether it changes your experience depends on how your workflow maps to the routing logic.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'd watch for reports from developers over the next few weeks about whether they notice model quality differences on different task types. That's the real-world data we don't have yet.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One practical thing worth flagging before we leave this story. If you're already on GitHub Copilot, Fusion is just there — no new subscription. The question is whether you'll notice the model switching at all, or whether it's invisible plumbing.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is exactly the trade-off. Convenience and optimization inside one ecosystem, or flexibility across multiple tools.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And invisible plumbing that touches your code quality is worth wanting to understand.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll allow it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay, I am UNREASONABLY excited about this one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Oh no.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Here we go.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: No, listen! You know that moment when a customer reports a bug, and then it just... disappears into a black hole of Slack messages and spreadsheets and nobody knows whose job it is?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I know that moment. I have LIVED that moment.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I have forwarded that email to the wrong person during that moment.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: RIGHT. So that chaos has a formal name — the case-to-bug process. Customer reports an issue, development team needs to fix it, and everything in between is a manual nightmare of miscommunication and delays.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So basically a game of broken telephone but the prize is a production outage.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. Now. Elements.cloud — they make business analysis software — had this exact problem. And in September 2025 they documented what happened when they plugged Salesforce Agentforce into that workflow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Agentforce being Salesforce's AI agent platform.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Gold star, yes. So instead of humans manually triaging every incoming case, the AI agent monitors cases as they arrive, analyzes them for technical context and relevance, and autonomously drives all the steps needed to hand a properly prepared issue to the development team. End to end.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: When you say autonomously drives the steps — what does that actually look like for the agent?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So it's not just reading a ticket and shrugging. It's ingesting the case details, applying context about what's technically relevant, sequencing the handover actions — basically doing the coordination work that previously lived in someone's inbox and everyone's memory.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Four weeks is a very short window to call something transformed. That's my challenge.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Fair, and Elements.cloud reports this from their own case study, so vendor-documented, take it accordingly. But the baseline they're measuring against is a genuinely chaotic manual process, not a slightly optimized one. The gap was wide enough that four weeks of improved speed and accuracy is at least plausible.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll allow it. Reluctantly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Very magnanimous of you, Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm a magnanimous person.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: This is the most agreement you two have shown all episode and it's about doubting me.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That tracks.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay but real question — someone listening who doesn't have a Salesforce environment, what do they actually do with this?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right, the limitation is real — you need that Salesforce infrastructure to replicate this specific build. But the idea transfers anywhere. Map your most common ticket-to-resolution workflow, find the one messy multi-step handover where information stalls and blame diffuses — and ask whether an AI agent could ingest that data and draft or execute the next action. That's your starting point. The payoff isn't the tool. It's finally knowing where the black hole actually is.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The opening question today: Google launched Gemini 4 Carbon with a staged rollout to cyber defenders. What does that actually mean and who can use it right now?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the capex story connects here in a way that's easy to miss. Two of the biggest AI spenders in the world just told investors they're not accelerating infrastructure growth. That's not a crisis, but it is a demand for efficiency. More deliberate model deployment, staged access, pricing designed for high-volume repetitive tasks — all of that fits a world where you're optimizing what you've built rather than just building more.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And Copilot Fusion is the developer-facing version of that pressure made concrete: GitHub says it reduces compute overhead by matching models to tasks — the efficiency is baked into the product design, not just the earnings call.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which might actually be better for end users if the routing works as described. The optimistic read on all three stories today is that we're seeing sophistication replace scale as the primary goal.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The cautious read is that we're seeing costs get managed in ways users can't fully see.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Both can be true.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: If your AI coding assistant could switch models to save you money, would you trust it to pick the right one for your code?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
